title: Pauri 23, meaning: the ant who remembers
hookLine: rivers flow into the sea without knowing its size; kings with mountains of wealth are not equal to an ant who remembers (Japji 23)

lines: WATCH AN ANT FOR A MINUTE.
cards: Have you ever watched an ant for a whole minute? Get down low on a sidewalk and follow one. It carries a crumb twice its size, loses it, finds it, goes around a pebble, keeps going.
It never looks up at the buildings or the traffic. It isn't impressed by anything. It just keeps its one thread.
Now picture a king on a golden throne, with vaults of treasure and armies at the gate. Which one matters more? You'd probably laugh.
Pauri 23 gives an answer that stops the laugh.

teach.b: The stanza opened: the praisers praise, but haven't grasped how great. Now it gives two pictures. First, in paraphrase: rivers and streams pour into the ocean without knowing how big it is.
They just flow in. That's anyone who praises: part of something they can't measure, pouring in anyway. The second picture turns the world's scale upside down.
Kings and emperors, with kingdoms as vast as oceans and wealth piled like mountains, are not equal to an ant, if the ant does not forget the One in its heart.
The word for ant is keeRee, one of the smallest living things anyone can see.
And the condition is simple: je tis manahu na veesarahi, if it does not forget Him in its mind.
The whole weight of the scale rests on that. The Sikh word for it is simran, remembrance, keeping the Name in mind through the day.

Pauri 23 says a creature the size of a grain of rice, if it remembers, outweighs every palace. That doesn't make wealth evil; plenty of Sikhs run businesses and work hard. It says what the scale is actually measuring.
Not size, not money, not how much you understand; the river doesn't understand the sea. Just whether you remember.
And that closes this stretch of Japji: bhareeai hath, as you sow, teerath tap, only the Maker knows, worlds beyond worlds, the praisers, and now the ant.
Two hundred days in, it's a good picture to carry: small, steady, remembering.

how: Pauri 23 is recited in the morning Japji Sahib; Sikhs practice simran, remembering the Name through the day, and often quote the ant of this stanza to say remembrance matters more than wealth or rank.

o: a long fast that cleans body and mind
a hymn sung aloud in the gurdwara
remembrance, keeping the Name in mind

games.q: what's inside Pauri 23 — tap the pairs.
p: pour in without knowing the sea

s: it says what the scale measures: not size or money, but remembering.
in Pauri 23, an ant who remembers outweighs kings
if it does not forget the One in its heart.
the rivers in Pauri 23 know how big the sea is
they pour in without knowing its size.

games.q: on one side, a king with mountains of wealth. on the other, an ant. what does Pauri 23 say tips the scale?
o: the ant, if it doesn't forget the One.
games.why: keeRee tul na hovanee je tis manahu na veesarahi: kings are not equal to an ant, if it does not forget Him in its mind.

practice: Watch something small: a leaf moving, a drop on a glass, a bug on the windowsill, or, if there's nothing, the small rise and fall of your own breath.
Give it your whole attention, the way the ant gives its whole attention to one crumb. Each time your mind wanders off to bigger things, come back to the small one.

wordCard.voice: Simran, remembrance. Rivers pour into a sea they can't measure; kings with mountains of wealth don't equal an ant that remembers.

orig.note: Gurmukhi: keeRee, an ant (the r is said with the tongue curled back); the small hero of Japji Pauri 23.

carryVoice: Your line: be the ant. Not the biggest on the scale, just the one who remembers. Day two hundred, done.
